title: DFS on Shibuya: Real Streets, Deep Routes ⚡
description: Watch Depth-First Search (DFS) dive through Shibuya’s street intersections like a stack, choosing a path and going all the way before backtracking. This visualization turns “dfs algorithm explained” into something you can literally see on a real map.
ig_caption:
Depth First Search (DFS) Traversal on Real Street Maps — what happens when DFS explores real city intersections ⚡

On Shibuya streets, we convert intersections → nodes and streets → edges, then run DFS as a graph traversal:
• Pick a start node (e.g., Shibuya Station area)
• Push neighbors in a chosen order
• Go deep until you hit a dead-end
• Backtrack, then continue until the traversal completes

The “magic” is in the call stack: DFS prioritizes depth over breadth, so the path looks wildly different than BFS—especially when multiple routes branch.

Takeaway: if you need to find *a* route fast in a tree-like graph, DFS can be effective; but if you need the *shortest* path, DFS isn’t the default choice.

Debate question: Should DFS prioritize left-to-right order, distance, or random neighbors on real maps? 👀
